# Education in Poland
In Poland, compulsory education begins at age six or seven with eight years of primary school (szkoła podstawowa), expanded from the previous six years following education reforms enacted in 2017 that abolished the three-year gimnazjum (junior high school). Upper secondary education includes general education at liceum (four years), leading to the Matura examination for university admission, and vocational education provided by technical schools (technikum) lasting five years or basic vocational schools lasting three years. The system accommodates special schools for students with disabilities, and higher education follows the Bologna framework with three-year bachelor’s and two-year master’s degrees; some professional degrees require longer programs. University grading uses a numeric scale from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (highest), with intermediate increments.
Polish students commonly study one or two foreign languages, with English and German being the most popular. Historical development emphasizes Poland’s longstanding educational tradition exemplified by the Jagiellonian University (founded in 1364), progressive reforms such as the 1999 and 2017 system restructurings, and the introduction of standardized curricula and exams. Compulsory education ends at age 18 after completing twelve years of schooling, integrating primary and secondary levels. The 2017 reforms returned to an 8+4/5 year structure for primary and secondary education, replacing the earlier 6+3+3 model.
